DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93, Module 3.

Terminal objective

1.0 Given an electrical print, READ and INTERPRET facility electrical diagrams and schematics. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.v

Enabling objectives

1.1 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering electrical drawings for the following components: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.v

  • a. Single-phase circuit breaker
  • b. Three-phase circuit breaker
  • c. Thermal overload
  • d. "a" contact
  • e. "b" contact
  • f. Time-delay contacts
  • g. Relay
  • h. Potential transformer
  • i. Current transformer
  • j. Single-phase transformer
  • k. Delta-wound transformer
  • l. Wye-wound transformer
  • m. Electric motor (open/closed)
  • n. Meters
  • o. Junctions (open/closed)
  • p. In-line fuses
  • q. Single switch
  • r. Multiple-position switch
  • s. Pushbutton switch
  • t. Limit switches
  • u. Turbine-driven generator
  • v. Motor-generator set
  • w. Generator (wye or delta)
  • x. Diesel-driven generator
  • y. Battery

1.2 Given an electrical drawing of a circuit containing a transformer, DETERMINE the direction of current flow, as shown by the transformer's symbol. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.v

1.3 IDENTIFY the symbols and/or codes used on engineering electrical drawings to depict the relationship between the following components: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.v

  • a. Relay and its contacts
  • b. Switch and its contacts
  • c. Interlocking device and its interlocked equipment

1.4 STATE the condition in which all electrical devices are shown, unless otherwise noted on the diagram or schematic. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.vi

1.5 Given a simple electrical schematic and initial conditions, DETERMINE the condition of the specified component (i.e., energized/de-energized, open/closed). DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.vi

1.6 Given a simple electrical schematic and initial conditions, IDENTIFY the power sources and/or loads and their status (i.e., energized or de-energized). DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.vi

Transformer symbols and polarity

Objectives 1.1, 1.2

Figure 1 (A) shows the basic transformer symbols, and Figure 1 (B) shows how they are modified for specific types and applications. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.2

Polarity marks are sometimes used to show current flow, which gives the phase relationship between the input and output terminals. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.2

"The marks usually appear as dots on a transformer symbol, as shown" DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.2
"On the primary side of the transformer the dot indicates current in; on the secondary side the dot indicates current out." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3
"If at a given instant the current is flowing into the transformer at the dotted end of the primary coil, it will be flowing out of the transformer at the dotted end of the secondary coil." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3

Knowledge check: Transformer symbols and polarity

Objective 1.2Q451

On a transformer polarity marking, what does the dot on the secondary side indicate?

The answer is C. On the primary side, the dot indicates current in; on the secondary, the dot indicates current out. DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 17

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1232

At a given instant, current flows into the dotted end of a transformer primary. What is the current doing at the dotted end of the secondary?

The answer is C. If current is flowing into the transformer at the dotted end of the primary coil, it will be flowing out of the transformer at the dotted end of the secondary coil. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3

Switches

Objectives 1.1

"The term "pole," as used to describe the switches in Figure 3, refers to the number of points at which current can enter a switch." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3
"The term "throw" used in Figure 3 refers to the number of circuits that each pole of a switch can complete or control." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3

A switch may have as many poles as it needs to perform its function. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.3

"Figure 4 provides the common symbols that are used to denote automatic switches and explains how the symbol indicates switch status or actuation." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.4

Fuses and breakers

Objectives 1.1

"In addition to the graphic symbol, most drawings will also provide the rating of the fuse next to the symbol." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.5

The rating is usually in amps. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.5

"When fuses, breakers, or switches are used in three-phase systems, the three-phase symbol combines the single-phase symbol in triplicate as shown in Figure 6." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.6

A removable breaker is a standard breaker symbol placed between a set of chevrons. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.6

"The chevrons represent the point at which the breaker disconnects from the circuit when removed." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.6

Relays, contacts, and other components

Objectives 1.1

"Figure 7 shows the common symbols for relays, contacts, connectors, lines, resistors, and other miscellaneous electrical components." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.6
  • "a" type contact (make): two parallel lines
  • "b" type contact (break): two parallel lines with a slash through them
  • TDC: time delay to close
  • TDO: time delay to open
  • Path junction: a dot where the lines meet
  • Meters: a circle marked V for voltmeter, A for ammeter, or OHM for ohmmeter

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.7

Large components

Objectives 1.1

"The symbols in Figure 8 are used to identify the larger components that may be found in an electrical diagram or schematic." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.7
"Usually the amount of detail will reflect the relative importance of a component to the particular diagram." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.7
  • Turbine driven generator: a triangle joined to a GEN circle, or a circle marked TG
  • Diesel driven generator: a box joined to a circle, or a circle marked DG
  • Motor generator: touching circles marked M and G
  • Battery: parallel long and short lines

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.8

Types of electrical diagrams

Objectives 1.0

"There are three ways to show electrical circuits." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.9

They are wiring, schematic, and pictorial diagrams. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.9

"The two most commonly used are the wiring diagram and the schematic diagram." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.9
  • Wiring diagrams emphasize connections between elements. Schematic diagrams emphasize the flow of the system.
  • Wiring diagrams use simplified pictorials that clearly resemble components. Schematic symbols show function but do not look like the equipment.
  • Wiring diagrams place equipment and wiring to approximate the actual physical location. Schematic layout shows the flow of the system as it functions.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.9

The pictorial diagram is usually not found in engineering applications, because it is not nearly as useful for repairing a circuit or finding how it operates. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.9

An electrical single line is a special schematic used for a large power distribution system. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.12

"This type of diagram depicts the major power sources, breakers, loads, and protective devices, thereby providing a useful overall view of the flow of power in a large electrical power distribution system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.12

On power distribution single lines, even for a 3-phase system, each load is commonly a simple circle with a description and its power rating. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.12

"Unless otherwise stated, the common units are kilowatts (kW)." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.12

Reading relays and contacts

Objectives 1.3, 1.4, 1.5

The condition of each component must be understood first. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

"For electrical schematics that detail individual relays and contacts, the components are always shown in the de-energized condition (also called the shelf- state)." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

Each relay is assigned a specific number and/or letter combination. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

"The number/letter code for each relay is carried by all associated contacts." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14
"If space permits, the relationship may be emphasized by drawing a dashed line (symbolizing a mechanical connection) between the relay and its contact(s) or a dashed box around them as shown in Figure 14 (B)." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

Figure 14 (C) shows a switch and a second set of contacts operated by that switch. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

Knowledge check: Reading relays and contacts

Objective 1.4Q1243

Unless otherwise noted, in what condition are devices shown on an electrical schematic?

The answer is D. Electrical components, such as relays, are drawn in the de-energized state unless otherwise noted on the diagram. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.17

Report a problem
Objective 1.3Q1244

How do you find the contacts operated by relay M1 on a schematic?

The answer is A. The number/letter code for each relay is carried by all associated contacts. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

Report a problem
Objective 1.3Q452

On electrical diagrams, what commonly shows the relationship between relays and other components?

The answer is D. Switches, relays, and interlocked equipment commonly use dashed lines or boxes to show the relationship between them and other components. DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 17

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1245

A relay coil on a schematic is energized. An "a" contact with its code is drawn open. What is that contact's state now?

The answer is C. Components are drawn in the de-energized condition, and the "a" type contact is a make contact, so energizing the relay closes it. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.14

Report a problem

Ganged switches and interlocks

Objectives 1.3, 1.5

A switch may contain several sets of contacts, or small internal switches, shown individually on a schematic. The position of one may affect another. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

"Such switches are called ganged switches and are symbolized by connecting them with a dashed line as shown in Figure 15 (A)." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15
"In that example, closing Switch 1 also closes Switch 2." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15
"The dashed line is also used to indicate a mechanical interlock between two circuit components." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Knowledge check: Ganged switches and interlocks

Objective 1.3Q1246

Two breakers on a drawing are joined by a dashed line. What does that show?

The answer is A. The dashed line is also used to indicate a mechanical interlock between two circuit components. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1247

Switch 1 and Switch 2 are ganged, and Switch 1 is closed. What is the state of Switch 2?

The answer is C. In the handbook example, closing Switch 1 also closes Switch 2. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Transformers on single lines

Objectives 1.1

"In system single line diagrams, transformers are often represented by the symbol for a single- phase air core transformer; however, that does not necessarily mean that the transformer has an air core or that it is single phase." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Single lines give only general functional information, like a P&ID for a piping system, so the reader must investigate further if more detail is needed. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

In three-phase diagrams, a small symbol may be placed beside the primary and secondary to show the type of windings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.16

Objective 1.1Q1248

A system single line shows a single-phase air core transformer symbol. What does that prove about the transformer?

The answer is B. That symbol does not necessarily mean that the transformer has an air core or that it is single phase. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1249

Which mark beside a transformer winding shows a delta connection?

The answer is D. Figure 16 shows a triangle for three-phase delta and a Y shape for three-phase wye. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.15

Worked examples

Objective 1.5

Read a schematic

Using this diagram, find its type, the fuse rating protecting the motor controller circuit, the component labeled ITDR in line 13, and the component at the far right of line 4.

  1. The diagram uses symbols with numbered lines between two power lines, so it is a schematic.
  2. The fuses in line 1 are marked 10.
  3. ITDR in line 13 is a time delay closing switch.
  4. The lamp at the far right of line 4 is marked G.

Answer: Schematic; 10 amps; a time delay closing switch; a green lamp.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.20

Objective 1.5

Trace switches and contacts

On the same schematic, which lines contain limit switches, and how many contacts are operated from relay 8CR?

  1. Limit switches are marked LS: 1LS through 6LS.
  2. Find every contact that carries the code 8CR.

Answer: Limit switches are in lines 7, 9, 11, 12, 14, and 15. Relay 8CR operates 4 contacts.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.20

Objective 1.6

Read a system diagram

Using this diagram, find its type, the voltage on the main bus, the circuit breaker type, and the component in the lower left corner.

  1. It shows the power sources, breakers, and loads of a system, so it is a system diagram.
  2. The main bus is labeled 4160 V.
  3. The chevrons on the breakers show they are drawout type.
  4. The circle in the lower left is fed through the 480/4160 V transformer.

Answer: System diagram; 4.16 kV or 4160 V; drawout type; an (emergency) diesel generator.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.22

Objective 1.6

Classify transformers

On the same diagram, how many current transformers are there, what voltage enters the transformer in the lower left corner, and how is the upper left transformer classified?

  1. Count the current transformers. The transformer in the upper right is a potential transformer, so it is not counted.
  2. The lower left transformer is marked 480/4160 V, and 480 V is the generator side.
  3. The upper left transformer has a delta mark on the primary and a grounded wye mark on the secondary.

Answer: 3 current transformers; 480 V; delta primary, grounded wye secondary.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.22

Summary

  • This chapter covered the common symbols used on electrical diagrams and schematics. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.17
  • Transformer polarity is shown by dots: the primary dot indicates current in, and the secondary dot indicates current out. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.17
  • Switches, relays, and interlocked equipment commonly use dashed lines or boxes to show their relationships. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.17
  • Electrical components, such as relays, are drawn in the de-energized state unless otherwise noted. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.17
  • This chapter reviewed the material in the module through practice reading examples. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-03 p.23
